title: Experimental quantum-computing-enhanced sensing using Grover's algorithm
authors: Mathieu Ouellet, Purnendu Sen, Xiangqin Wang, Saswata Roy, Xingrui Song, Vladimir Kremenetski, Sridhar Prabhu, Valla Fatemi, Peter L. McMahon
abstract: The combination of quantum sensing with quantum computing to provide an enhancement over conventional quantum sensing has recently emerged as a promising potential application of quantum computing that could give advantages without needing large-scale or fault-tolerant hardware. In this work, we report an experimental demonstration of a recent theoretical proposal to repurpose Grover's search algorithm to improve the ability to detect signals with unknown frequency within a large detection bandwidth. Our experiments were based on a system comprising a single superconducting qubit coupled to a single superconducting cavity, highlighting the modest hardware requirements for realizing the protocol. We found that Grover-based sensing was able to outperform the natural non-Grover baseline for our experimental platform for detection bandwidths $>$10~MHz, with an advantage that empirically grew superlinearly with the bandwidth beyond that break-even point. The use of the Grover-based protocol reduced the amount of signal that needed to be sensed to make an accurate detection decision by more than 10$\times$ for choices of larger detection bandwidth and higher desired detection accuracy. Our results provide a proof-of-principle validation that Grover-based quantum computational sensing can be realized in near-term hardware and provide a metrological advantage well beyond break-even in spite of the additional protocol complexity.
summary: This paper reports an experimental demonstration of using Grover's algorithm to enhance quantum sensing for detecting unknown frequencies in large bandwidths. By repurposing the search algorithm for amplitude amplification in a superconducting qubit-cavity system, the researchers achieved a significant reduction in the required signal resources compared to standard methods. This validates the use of quantum computation for practical, near-term quantum metrology.
main_problem: To experimentally demonstrate how repurposing Grover's search algorithm can enhance the detection of unknown frequency signals within a large bandwidth, surpassing conventional quantum sensing limits.
main_result: Grover-based sensing outperformed the natural baseline for bandwidths greater than 10 MHz, achieving a reduction in required sensed signal by over 10 times for high accuracy.
method: The protocol uses Grover's amplitude amplification in the cavity Fock-state basis, followed by a number-selective qubit $\pi$-pulse to convert the amplified state population into a measurable qubit excitation probability.
model_or_system: The experiment is performed on a superconducting circuit comprising a single transmon qubit dispersively coupled to a single superconducting cavity.
key_observables: Qubit-excitation probability, sensing bandwidth ($\Delta f$), and the total number of signal interrogations required for a given accuracy.
important_parameters: Detection bandwidth ($\Delta f$), Grover iteration count ($N$), and the crossover bandwidth (around 10 MHz).
main_assumptions: The protocol is presented as a proof-of-principle demonstration, and the analysis relies on fitting distributions (Poisson, Gaussian) to measured data.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the overall sensing process, the dependence of qubit excitation probability on Grover iterations, and comparisons of required signal resources versus bandwidth for different protocol choices.
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical proposal, presents the experimental platform (qubit-cavity system), calibrates system parameters (dispersive shift, displacement amplitude), and finally compares the resource scaling of Grover-enhanced sensing against non-Grover baselines.
why_interesting: This work directly applies quantum computation principles (Grover's algorithm) to a physical quantum optics system (cavity QED), demonstrating a measurable metrological advantage in a near-term hardware setting.
